criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1. Although SDG 6.1 and drinking-water access in Sub-Saharan Africa are cited as background motivation, the study empirically examines project-level capital financing and stakeholder-perceived overall performance of water supply projects rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Fails Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Plain wording: Although the introduction and theoretical framework mention water policy and governance as background/mediating concepts, the empirical analysis tests only corporate/project capital financing strategies (internal funds, bank debt, equity, mezzanine, and donor grants, aggregated into a single Likert-scale score) and explicitly notes on p. 12 that it does not account for government policy influence or donor conditions; furthermore, even if donor/project financing were stretched under plain institutional wording, the study still fails c1 and c4, so plain_criterion2_decision is exclude. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Project capital financing mix and generic project delivery/feasibility are not rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanisms directly governing household or community service access (not eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, user tariff/cost-recovery rules governing access, discretion, enforcement, or utility regulatory structure governing access).
criterion_notes.c3: Satisfies Criterion 3. Mixed-methods primary empirical study combining structured Likert-scale survey data from 457 project stakeholders (analyzed via Pearson correlation and simple linear regression, Tables 1-3) with thematic analysis of key informant interviews.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4. The dependent variable is an aggregate stakeholder Likert-scale perception score labeled 'Performance of Water Supply Projects' (with qualitative discussion of project feasibility and financial sustainability). No specific household or community outcome measuring water access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is reported.
criterion_notes.c5: Satisfies Criterion 5 sufficiently to classify scope. The study design (mixed-methods cross-sectional descriptive and correlational survey plus key informant interviews), respondent sample (457 project stakeholders in Nyanza Region, Kenya), exposure (composite Likert-scale score for project financing strategies), and outcome (composite Likert-scale score for performance of water supply projects) are identifiable, even though the article omits the sampling frame, number of projects/interviews, and individual questionnaire items.
criterion_notes.c6: Satisfies Criterion 6. Full text is in English (with abstracts in English, Portuguese, and Spanish).

evidence_quotes.quote: The primary objective of this study was to examine the extent to which project financing strategies affect the performance of water supply projects in the Nyanza Region of Kenya.

This study examines how different financing strategies—equity, bank debt, mezzanine, and donor financing—affect the performance of water supply projects, with an emphasis on risk management and water policy as moderating and mediating factors, respectively

Furthermore, the study does not explicitly account for the external constraints noted in critiques of the theory, such as donor conditions or government policy influence, which are common in developing regions like Nyanza.
A mixed methods research design was employed, combining quantitative analysis from 457 project stakeholders using structured questionnaires and qualitative data from key informant interviews.

Simple linear regression was adopted to investigate the effect of Project Financing Strategies and Performance of Water Supply Projects. It was necessary to get the views of the participants on the effect of Project Financing Strategies and Performance of Water Supply Projects.

raw_response.exposure: Project financing strategies (conceptualized as internal funds, bank debt, equity, mezzanine, and donor grant financing, operationalized quantitatively as a composite Likert-scale perception score)
raw_response.outcome: Performance of water supply projects (operationalized quantitatively as an aggregate stakeholder-rated Likert-scale perception score; specific sub-indicators not reported)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 457 water supply project stakeholders in Nyanza Region, Kenya (structured Likert-scale questionnaires; df total = 456) plus key informant interviewees (count not reported)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude (E03 - Wrong exposure; also lacks a household/community service-access outcome under c1/c4). This mixed-methods survey of 457 project stakeholders in Nyanza Region, Kenya examines how project capital financing strategies (internal funds, bank debt, equity, mezzanine, and donor grants) relate to stakeholder-perceived overall 'performance of water supply projects.' Although water policy is mentioned in theoretical background, only the composite 'Project Financing Strategies' variable is empirically tested (Tables 1-3), and p. 12 explicitly notes that government policy influence and donor conditions were not accounted for. It does not examine any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance rule-type mechanism governing water service access (Criterion 2), nor does it measure a household or community service-access outcome (Criteria 1 and 4). Excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods cross-sectional descriptive and correlational survey with key informant interviews
